evidence_set: SUDORS, January 2021–June 2024, 49 states and DC (jurisdictions had to report at least 75% of their overdose deaths in at least one 6-month period; California and Wisconsin were included for part of the period, Texas and Wyoming only for January–June 2024, North Dakota not included): of 309,274 unintentional or undetermined-intent overdose deaths, 96,614 (31.2%) involved methamphetamine, meaning that the medical examiner or coroner listed it as a cause of death on the death certificate, in their report or in the postmortem toxicology report; 66,475 (68.8% of these; 21.5% of all deaths) also involved opioids and 30,139 (9.7% of all deaths) did not. Any stimulant: 182,502 (59.0%), 73.0% of them with opioids.

Among methamphetamine-involved deaths with circumstance data (46 states and DC; 67,831 deaths), those without opioids more often had a known history of cardiovascular disease (hypertension excluded; 39.3% vs 19.8%) and were more often seen in an emergency department for the fatal overdose (30.3% vs 17.4%), and less often had evidence of opioid use (12.2% vs 41.1%). Among all methamphetamine-involved deaths (49 states and DC), those without opioids were older (aged 45–54, 55–64 and 65 or older: 27.1%, 27.9% and 9.2% vs 21.3%, 14.3% and 3.2%). The authors expect stimulant-involved deaths to be underestimated: some are certified with cardiovascular causes and get no overdose code, and postmortem toxicology varies and does not routinely test for emerging stimulants.
